articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets entities and individuals deemed to be supporting Iran's illicit activities.

These designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing behavior in the region and its pursuit of prohibited weapons programs. The specific details of the designated parties and the nature of their involvement were not immediately released but are expected to be detailed in accompanying guidance.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber, TCO, and Cuba-Related Entities; Publishes Cuba Determination
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related malicious actors, transnational criminal organizations, and entities linked to Cuba. This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating a range of threats to national security and foreign policy.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also published a Cuba-related determination, providing further clarity on the scope and application of existing sanctions against the Cuban regime. The specific entities and individuals targeted were not immediately detailed, but such designations typically result in asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

China's Ministry of Commerce expressed strong opposition to the US sanctions imposed on two Chinese companies on November 5, citing their alleged involvement with Cuba. Beijing views these measures as unilateral and a violation of international law, harming Chinese companies' interests and the stability of bilateral economic relations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing Iran-related listings on November 4, 2026. These actions aim to further pressure the Iranian regime by targeting its financial networks and support structures.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related alert to inform the public about potential evasion tactics and compliance obligations. The agency also issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question, providing updated guidance for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License
body: On October 29, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment provides updated authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Iranian sanctions program.

The specific changes within the amended General License aim to clarify permissible activities or adjust existing authorizations, reflecting ongoing policy considerations regarding humanitarian aid, personal remittances, or other specific sectors.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates North Korea and DRC-Related Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions are part of broader U.S. efforts to address proliferation financing, human rights abuses, and regional instability.

The North Korea designations aim to disrupt the regime's illicit revenue generation and weapons programs, while the DRC-related designations target those contributing to conflict and corruption within the country. The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately available.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: On October 26, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These updates provide additional guidance and clarification for financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations under OFAC regulations.

The amendments aim to enhance understanding of reporting requirements and the proper procedures for handling transactions involving sanctioned parties or jurisdictions. This ongoing refinement of guidance helps ensure effective implementation of U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran, Russia General Licenses; Removes Belarus, North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses on October 21, 2026. These licenses authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, reflecting specific policy adjustments.

Concurrently, OFAC removed several designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a reassessment of sanctions targets in those regions. The agency also issued amended Frequently Asked Questions to provide further clarity on these new and updated measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Under PAIPA, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: On October 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target entities and individuals involved in the theft of American intellectual property, a critical national security and economic concern.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses to mitigate any unintended consequences and ensure that legitimate activities can continue. The PAIPA designations mark a significant step in the U.S. government's efforts to protect its technological and economic advantages.
China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) rejected the allegations of trade secret theft, stating that the progress of Chinese AI companies is due to sustained investment in research and innovation.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ

The amendment aims to clarify permissible activities or adjust existing authorizations under the Venezuela sanctions program, reflecting ongoing policy considerations and humanitarian concerns.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty is part of coordinated enforcement actions against the bank, which also included a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million penalty from the OCC.

The penalties stem from the bank's willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), including missing or delaying the detection and reporting of over $5 billion in suspicious activity. OFAC's action highlights the critical importance of robust sanctions compliance programs within financial institutions.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 10, 2027
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has extended the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027. This rule, originally set to take effect on November 10, 2026, expands export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to companies owned or controlled by parties on certain restricted party lists.

The suspension, which was initially implemented in November 2025 as part of a trade understanding with China, aims to provide additional time for businesses to adapt to the expanded compliance obligations. The Affiliates Rule is modeled on OFAC's '50% Rule,' prohibiting export trade with companies directly or indirectly owned 50% or more by sanctioned parties.

This extension, published in the Federal Register on November 9, 2026, means that the license requirements and related provisions from the Affiliates Rule will not be reimposed until January 10, 2027, unless BIS takes further action. The rule significantly increases compliance obligations and enforcement risk for companies with international operations, particularly those with connections to China.
articles.source: Federal Register / Benesch Law / ovrseas / Kharon / MLQ.ai / Deloitte

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced last week that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aligns export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms. Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons.

License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors. Jeffrey I. Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, stated that this move alleviates compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
